blocks.prompt: Read this out loud
blocks.text: An astronaut goes to space. Space is very high up. There is no air in space. So the astronaut wears a big white suit. The suit has a helmet. The helmet holds air to breathe. In space there is no up and no down. The astronaut floats. Her water floats. Her pencil floats. At bedtime she zips into a sleeping bag. The bag is tied to the wall. Now she will not float away.

blocks.prompt: Everything Floats
blocks.text: Astronaut means star sailor. It comes from two old Greek words. Up in space there is no up and no down. Everything floats. A spoon floats. A drop of juice floats into a wobbly ball. That is why astronauts eat off sticky tortillas instead of bread. Bread makes crumbs, and floating crumbs can get into a machine. Their salt and pepper come as drops of water, not powder. At night they climb into a sleeping bag that is clipped to the wall. If they did not clip it, they would drift around the room all night and bump into things.

because bread makes crumbs that float into machines
so they do not drift around the room at night

blocks.prompt: A Spaceship Shaped Like a Person
blocks.text: A spacesuit is not clothing. It is a small spaceship shaped like a person. Space has no air at all. No air means nothing to breathe, and it also means no pressure pushing on your skin. Your body needs that push. So the suit does both jobs. It holds pure oxygen inside and squeezes the astronaut gently, the way the air does down here on the ground. The suit has other jobs too. In sunlight, the outside of the suit can reach about 250 degrees Fahrenheit. In shadow, it drops to about 250 degrees below zero. The suit has layers to block the heat and the cold, and it runs cool water through tubes in a stretchy undershirt to carry away body heat. The gold coating on the visor is real gold, spread thinner than a human hair, and it blocks the harshest sunlight. A NASA spacesuit weighs around 280 pounds on Earth. In orbit it weighs nothing at all, and an astronaut can work outside for eight hours without ever taking it off.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Astronauts float because they are falling
The station orbits about 250 miles up
Gravity up there is still about 90 percent as strong
It moves sideways at about 17,500 miles per hour
One lap around Earth every 90 minutes
That is 16 sunrises every day

blocks.prompt: Why Astronauts Float (It Is Not What You Think)
blocks.text: Here is a question that sounds simple. Why do astronauts float? The usual answer is that there is no gravity in space. That answer is wrong. The International Space Station orbits about 250 miles above the ground, and at that height Earth's gravity is still about ninety percent as strong as it is in your kitchen. If gravity switched off up there, the station would sail away in a straight line and never come back. The real answer is stranger. The station is falling. It has been falling since the day it was built, and it never lands, because it is also moving sideways at about 17,500 miles per hour. Picture throwing a ball. Throw it gently and it curves down and hits the ground. Throw it harder and it lands further away. Throw it hard enough and the ground curves away beneath it just as fast as the ball drops. The ball keeps falling and keeps missing. That is an orbit. That is all an orbit is. The astronauts inside are falling too, at exactly the same rate as the walls, the floor, and their own dinner. Nothing presses up against them, so nothing feels like weight. They are not weightless because gravity is gone. They are weightless because everything around them is falling together. Scientists call this free fall, and it is why the station circles the whole planet every ninety minutes.

blocks.prompt: Answer each question in full sentences.

The passage says the station would sail away in a straight line if gravity switched off. What does that tell you gravity is actually doing?
answers: that there is no gravity in space; gravity at that height is still about ninety percent as strong
(falling forward fast enough that you keep missing the ground as it curves away)
she is falling at the same rate as everything around her, so nothing presses against her
(inference: gravity is bending the station's straight path into a circle)

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Bones lose about 1 percent of density per month
Fluid shifts up: puffy face, skinny legs
The spine stretches about two inches taller
Around two hours of exercise every day
Weights are useless, so machines use vacuum cylinders
Many are carried out of the capsule on landing

blocks.prompt: A Body Built for a Planet
blocks.text: Astronauts often say the hardest part of space is not getting there. It is what space does to you while you stay. A human body is built for a planet. Every system inside it assumes that gravity is pulling down, and the body spends its whole life pushing back. Remove that pull and the body does something sensible and unhelpful: it stops paying for equipment it no longer seems to need. Bones go first. Weight-bearing bones in the hips and legs lose about one percent of their density every month in orbit, which is roughly what an older person on Earth loses in a year. Muscles shrink for the same reason, because nothing is asking them to work. Blood and other fluids, no longer pulled toward the feet, drift up into the chest and head. Astronauts arrive in orbit with puffy faces and skinny legs. Their bodies read the extra fluid in the chest as a sign of too much blood and quietly get rid of some, so a returning astronaut can be short on blood without knowing it. The spine, freed from carrying the head all day, stretches out, and most astronauts grow about two inches taller in orbit. They shrink again within days of landing. The countermeasure is exercise, and it is not optional. Crew on the space station work out around two hours a day, strapped by harness onto a treadmill or hauling on a machine that uses vacuum cylinders instead of free weights, because free weights would weigh nothing. That regimen is why modern astronauts come home in far better shape than early crews did. Even so, landing is brutal. After months of falling, an astronaut who stands up too quickly can faint, because the heart has forgotten how hard it must push to lift blood to a brain that is suddenly above it. Many are carried from the capsule and sit down for their first photograph home. The gravity they grew up in feels, for a few days, like a hand pressing on their chest.

6.title: The Star Sailors Who Never Stop Falling
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Star Sailors Who Never Stop Falling

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Astronaut: Greek astron plus nautes, star sailor
Russian term: cosmonaut, sailor of the universe
2017 class: 18,000 applied, 12 selected
The training pool holds six million gallons
About seven hours underwater per hour of spacewalk
The overview effect, named by Frank White in 1987

blocks.prompt: Star Sailor: The Job Behind the Word
blocks.text: Ask a seven year old what an astronaut does and you will get a clean answer: they fly to space. Ask an astronaut and the answer gets complicated, because flying to space is the smallest part of the job by a wide margin. Start with the word. Astronaut is stitched together from two ancient Greek pieces, astron and nautes, and it means star sailor. It is a romantic name for what is, most days, a technical one. The Russians chose cosmonaut, sailor of the universe, which is no less grand. Both words were coined before anyone had done the thing, and both promise adventure. The reality that followed is more interesting than the promise. Selection is the first filter and it is savage. For the astronaut class announced in 2017, more than 18,000 people applied. Twelve were chosen. The twelve were not chosen for bravery, which is difficult to test and easy to fake. They were chosen for a duller set of qualities: an advanced degree in a hard science or engineering, a thousand hours flying jets or years of professional technical work, and the ability to stay useful and pleasant while locked in a small room with the same five people for months. NASA screens for the person who does not become a problem. Then comes the training, which is where the years actually go. Candidates learn Russian, because the Soyuz spacecraft and half the station are labeled in it. They fly jets. They practice medical procedures on each other. Above all, they go into the pool. The Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory in Houston holds six million gallons of water and a full sized mockup of the space station, and astronauts rehearse spacewalks in it while divers add or remove weights to hold them neither sinking nor rising. The rule of thumb is about seven hours underwater for every single hour they will eventually spend outside. A spacewalk that lasts an afternoon is the visible tip of a year of Tuesdays. And the mission itself, once it finally arrives, looks less like exploration than like maintenance. Astronauts on the station fix toilets. They swap out air filters. They run experiments designed by scientists on the ground, following procedures written by other people, and they photograph the results. They exercise for two hours because their skeletons are quietly dissolving. It is skilled, careful, repetitive work performed inside a pressurized tube that is falling around the planet at five miles per second. So why does the word still carry its old shine? Because of what happens at the window. In 1987 the writer Frank White gave a name to something astronauts had been describing since the first crews: the overview effect. Seen from orbit, the Earth has no borders on it. The atmosphere resolves into a thin blue seam, visibly thin, and every war and every argument sits underneath it. Astronaut after astronaut, including hard headed test pilots with no interest in poetry, has come home changed by it and struggled to explain why. That is the honest shape of the job. Years of preparation, months of maintenance, and a handful of moments at a window that rearrange a person. The star sailor name turned out to be right, though not for the reasons anyone expected.
